To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) cloud computing is based upon the concepts of anycast routing and data center virtualisation, (ii) these concepts bring new challenges to optical network planning, and (iii) column generation can be adopted to tackle the new challenges.

(i) the network dimensioning problem for cloud computing based applications is significantly different compared to classical RWA; and (ii) column generation is a promising approach to tackle such problems.

“cloud computing applications, such as anycast routing and data center virtualisation, can be exploited in the planning of resilient optical cloud networks by using large scale optimisation methods, which lead to significant capacity savings”.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of dimensioning algorithms for optical cloud networks.
the design and dimensioning of optical clouds, i.e., optical wide area networks that are specifically tailored towards the requirements of cloud computing.
how to dimension optical networks to support cloud computing, and how to optimally exploit the cloud concepts for capacity saving.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cloud computing is a major challenge for optical network planning, which is not yet solved.
the cloud computing era brings about new challenges in the dimensioning of optical networks, and that column generation is a promising technique for addressing these challenges.
the network planning for optical clouds has to be done with a different mindset compared to the traditional RWA methods.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cloud paradigm brings about a new way of dimensioning optical networks, which is fundamentally different from the traditional RWA problem, and that column generation can be adopted to solve the resulting large scale problems.
we have shown that cloud computing can be a powerful tool to improve the network performance, and in particular the resilience.
the cloud is a promising concept for future optical network planning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cloud computing can be used to significantly increase the efficiency of optical networks.
the network dimensioning for optical clouds can be formulated as a mixed integer program, which can be solved efficiently by column generation.
the network dimensioning methodology needs to take the particular characteristics of cloud computing into account, and that this can be achieved by applying large scale optimization.
